text:
1.24 g of $AX_{2} ($molar mass 124 g mol$^{−1})$ is dissolved in 1 kg of water to form a solution with boiling point of 100.0156°C, while 25.4 g of $AY_{2} ($molar mass 250 g mol$^{−1})$ in 2 kg of water constitutes a solution with a boiling point of 100.0260°C.
$K_{b}(H_{2}O) = 0.52 kg$ mol$^{−1}$
Which of the following is correct?
options: $AX_{2}$ is completely unionised while $AY_{2}$ is fully ionised.
$AX_{2}$ is fully ionised while $AY_{2}$ is completely unionised.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Mass of $Ax_{2}=1.24\mathrm{g}$ (solute)

Molarmass of $AX_{2}=124\mathrm{g}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$

Mass of water $=1\mathrm{kg}$ (solvent.)

Boiling point of water $=100^{\circ }\mathrm{C}$

Boiling point of water after adding solute $AX_{2}=100.0156^{\circ }\mathrm{C}$

Mass of $AY_{2}=25.4\mathrm{g}$ (solute)

Molarmass of $AY_{2}=250\mathrm{g}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$

Mass of water $=2\mathrm{kg}$ (Solvent)

Boiling point of water $=100^{\circ }\mathrm{C}$

Boiling point of water after adding solute $Ay_{2}=100.0260^{\circ }\mathrm{C}$
 $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{b}}(\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O})=0.52\mathrm{K}\mathrm{kg}\mathrm{mol}{}^{-1}=0.520^{\circ }\mathrm{C}\mathrm{kg}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$

The ionisation of $Ax_{2}$ and $AY_{2}$ can be determined by calculating Van't Hoff factor.

The phenomenon given in the question is elevation in boiling point. The boiling point of solvent increases when another compound (solute) is added to it.

Relation: $\Delta T_{b}=K_{b}\cdot i\cdot m$

$\Delta T_{b}=T_{b}-T_{b}^{0}$

$\Delta T_{b}\to$ Boiling point elevation

$T_{b}\to$ Boiling point of solution (solvent + solute)

$T_{b}^{0}\to$ Boiling point of solvent

$K_{b}\to$ Molal elevation constant

$i\to$ Van't Hoff factor

$m\to \text{Molality}=\frac{\text{Number of moles}}{\mathrm{kg}\text{of solvent}},\text{Moles}=\frac{\text{Mass}}{\text{Molarmass}}$

For $AX_{2}$ and $AY_{2}$ (solute), Van't Hoff factor represents how many particles a solute dissociates into when dissolved in a solvent (water).

For non-electrolytes, $i=1$

$\begin{array}{l} \begin{array}{l} AX_{2}: \\ \text{Moles}=\dfrac{\text{mass}}{\text{molarmass}}=\dfrac{1.24\mathrm{g}}{124\mathrm{g}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}}=0.01\mathrm{mol} \\ \text{Molality}=\dfrac{\text{Moles}}{k_{g}\text{of solvent}}=\dfrac{0.01\mathrm{mol}}{1\mathrm{kg}}=0.01\mathrm{mol}\mathrm{kg}^{-1} \\ \Delta T_{b}=K_{b}\times i\times m \\ i=\dfrac{\Delta T_{b}}{k_{b}\times m} \\ =\dfrac{T_{b}-T_{b}^{0}}{K_{b}\times m} \end{array} \\ \text{Substitute values as.,} \end{array}$

$\begin{array}{ll} i & =\dfrac{(100.0156^{\circ }\mathrm{C}-100^{\circ }\mathrm{C})}{0.52^{\circ }\mathrm{C}\mathrm{kg}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}\times 0.01\mathrm{mol}\mathrm{kg}^{-1}} \\ ~=\dfrac{0.0156^{\circ }\mathrm{C}}{0.52\times 0.01{}^{\circ }\mathrm{C}}=3 \end{array}$

$i=3$ means, there are 3 particles in solution after $AX_{2}$ dissolved in water.

$Ax_{2}\to 1A^{+}+2X^{-}(1+2=3)$

$\begin{array}{l} Ax_{2}\text{is completely ionised.} \\ AY_{2}: \end{array}$

$\begin{array}{lllll} \begin{array}{ll} \text{Moles} & =\dfrac{\text{Mass}}{\text{Molarmass}}=\dfrac{25.4\mathrm{g}}{250\mathrm{g}\mathrm{mol}}=0.1016\mathrm{mol} \\ \text{Molality} & =\dfrac{\text{Moles}}{\mathrm{kgof}^{-1}\text{solvent}}=\dfrac{0.1016\mathrm{mol}}{2\mathrm{kg}}=0.0508\mathrm{mol}\mathrm{kg}^{-1} \\ \Delta T_{b} & =k_{b}\times i\times m \\ i & =\dfrac{\Delta T_{b}}{k_{b}\times m} \\ =\dfrac{T_{b}-T_{b}^{0}}{k_{b}\times m} \end{array} \\ \text{Substitute values as,} \end{array}$

$i=\frac{(100.0260^{\circ }C-100^{\circ }C)}{0.52^{\circ }Ckgmol^{-1}\times 0.0508molkg^{-1}}$

$=\frac{0.0260^{\circ }\mathrm{C}}{0.52\times 0.0508^{\circ }\mathrm{C}}$

$=0.98$

$\approx 1$

$i=1$ means $AY_{2}$ is completely unionised.

$Ay_{2}$ not give ionised particles when dissolved in water.

So, $AX_{2}$ is completely ionised and $AY_{2}$ is completely unionised.

Answer: Option 4) $Ax_{2}$ is fully ionised, $AY_{2}$ is completely unionised.

solution.body:
$Mg\left |Mg^{2+}(aq)\right |_{(Anode)}|Ag^{+}(aq)|Ag_{(Cathode)}$

Nernst equation (general)

$E_{Cell}=E_{Cell}^{0}-\frac{RT}{nF}\ln Q$

$\mathrm{Mg}_{(\mathrm{s})}+2\mathrm{Ag}_{(\text{aq})}^{+}⟶\mathrm{Mg}_{(\text{aq})}^{2+}+2\mathrm{Ag}(\mathrm{s})$

$n$ (number of electrons transferred $)=2$

Concentration of solid species

text:
The correct increasing order of stability of the complexes based on $\Delta _{0}$ value is :

I. $[\text{Mn}(\text{CN})_{6}]^{3-}$

II. $[\text{Co}(\text{CN})_{6}]^{4-}$

III. $[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_{6}]^{4-}$

IV. $[\text{Fe}(\text{CN})_{6}]^{3-}$
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
$\mathrm{CN}{}^{-}$ is a strong-field ligand, so all four complexes are low spin, and the crystal field stabilisation energy is $\text{CFSE}=\left (-0.4n_{t_{2g}}+0.6n_{e_{g}}\right )\Delta _{0}$.

I. $[\mathrm{Mn}(\mathrm{CN}){}_{6}]{}^{3-}$: $\mathrm{Mn}{}^{3+}$, $d^{4}$, $t_{2g}^{4}e_{g}^{0}$, $\text{CFSE}=-1.6\Delta _{0}$.

II. $[\mathrm{Co}(\mathrm{CN}){}_{6}]{}^{4-}$: $\mathrm{Co}{}^{2+}$, $d^{7}$, $t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{1}$, $\text{CFSE}=-2.4\Delta _{0}+0.6\Delta _{0}=-1.8\Delta _{0}$.

III. $[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN}){}_{6}]{}^{4-}$: $\mathrm{Fe}{}^{2+}$, $d^{6}$, $t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{0}$, $\text{CFSE}=-2.4\Delta _{0}$.

IV. $[\mathrm{Fe}(\mathrm{CN}){}_{6}]{}^{3-}$: $\mathrm{Fe}{}^{3+}$, $d^{5}$, $t_{2g}^{5}e_{g}^{0}$, $\text{CFSE}=-2.0\Delta _{0}$.

Stability rises with the magnitude of CFSE: $1.6\Delta _{0}<1.8\Delta _{0}<2.0\Delta _{0}<2.4\Delta _{0}$, so the order is I < II < IV < III.

Hence, the correct option is (A).
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift

text: 500 J of energy is transferred as heat to 0.5 mol of Argon gas at 298 K and 1.00 atm. The final temperature and the change in internal energy respectively are: Given: $R = 8.3 J K^{-1}$ mol$^{-1}$
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Amount of energy transferred as heat, $Q=500\mathrm{J}$

Number of moles of Argon, $n=0.5\mathrm{mol}$

Temperature (Initial), $T_{i}=298\mathrm{K}$

Pressure, $P=1.00\mathrm{atm}$

Final temperature, $T_{F}=$ ?

Change in internal energy, $\Delta U=$ ?

$R=8.3\mathrm{J}\mathrm{K}^{-1}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}$

For a constant pressure process, the heat added is related to the temperature changes as

$Q=nC_{p}\Delta T$ ....... (1)

$\begin{array}{l} \text{Also, the change in internal energy formula is} \\ \Delta U=nC_{V}\Delta T-(2)\text{.... (2)} \end{array}$

$\begin{array}{lll} \text{For monoatomic gas (Argon),} \\ \begin{array}{ll} C_{v} & =\dfrac{3}{2}R \\ \text{So,}C_{p} & =C_{v}+R(C_{p}-C_{v}=R) \\ =\dfrac{3}{2}R+R=\dfrac{5}{2}R \end{array} \end{array}$

$\begin{array}{l} \text{In equation (1)}\Rightarrow  \\ \begin{array}{l} Q=nC_{p}\Delta T \\ Q=nC_{p}(T_{F}-T_{i}) \\ 500\mathrm{J}=0.5\mathrm{mol}\times \dfrac{5}{2}R(T_{F}-T_{i})R=8.3\mathrm{JK}^{-1}\mathrm{mol}^{-1} \\ 500\mathrm{J}=0.5\mathrm{mol}\times \dfrac{5}{2}\times 8.3\mathrm{J}K^{-1}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}(T_{F}-T_{i}) \end{array} \end{array}$

$T_{F}-T_{i}=\frac{500\mathrm{J}}{0.5\mathrm{mol}\times \frac{5}{2}\times 8.3\text{J K}^{-1}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}}$

$\begin{array}{ll} =\dfrac{500}{0.5\times \frac{5}{2}\times 8.3}\mathrm{k} \\ =48.2\mathrm{k} \\ T_{F} & =48.2\mathrm{k}+298\mathrm{k} \\ =346.2\mathrm{k} \\ \approx 348\mathrm{k} \end{array}$

$\begin{array}{ll} \text{In equation (2)}\Rightarrow  \\ \begin{array}{ll} \Delta U & =nC_{V}\Delta T \\ =0.5\mathrm{mol}\times \dfrac{3}{2}R\times 48.2\mathrm{K} \\ =0.5\mathrm{mol}\times \dfrac{3}{2}\times 8.3\mathrm{J}\mathrm{K}^{-1}\mathrm{mol}^{-1}\times 48.2\mathrm{K} \\ =300.045\mathrm{J}\approx 300\mathrm{J} \end{array} \end{array}$

The final temperature is, 348 k

change in internal energy is 300 J

So, correct answer is Option 2) 348 K and 300 J

text: The correct option with order of melting points of the pairs (Mn, Fe), (Tc, Ru) and (Re, Os) is :
options: Fe < Mn, Ru < Tc and Re < Os
Fe < Mn, Ru < Tc and Os < Re
Mn < Fe, Tc < Ru and Re < Os
Mn < Fe, Tc < Ru and Os < Re
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
In each transition series the melting points rise to a maximum at about $d^{5}$ and then fall regularly as the d electrons pair up, except for the anomalously low values of Mn and Tc, whose stable half-filled d sets take less part in metallic bonding.

Mn ($3d^{5}4s^{2}$, about $1246{}^{\circ }\text{C}$) therefore melts below Fe (about $1538{}^{\circ }\text{C}$): $\mathrm{Mn}<\mathrm{Fe}$.

Tc ($4d^{5}5s^{2}$, about $2157{}^{\circ }\text{C}$) likewise melts below Ru (about $2334{}^{\circ }\text{C}$): $\mathrm{Tc}<\mathrm{Ru}$.

Re and Os follow the regular fall after the maximum at W (about $3422{}^{\circ }\text{C}$): Re (about $3186{}^{\circ }\text{C}$) melts above Os (about $3033{}^{\circ }\text{C}$), so $\mathrm{Os}<\mathrm{Re}$.

Hence, the correct option is (D).
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift

text:
The reaction $A_{2}+B_{2}\to 2AB$ follows the mechanism:
$A_{2}⇌_{k_{-1}}^{k_{1}}A+A$ (fast)
$A+B_{2}\leftarrow ^{k_{2}}AB+B$ (slow)
$A+B\to AB$ (fast)
The overall order of the reaction is:
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The slow step is rate determining:

$\text{rate}=k_{2}[\mathrm{A}][\mathrm{B}{}_{2}]$

A is an intermediate, so its concentration comes from the fast pre-equilibrium $\mathrm{A}{}_{2}2\mathrm{A}$:

$\dfrac{k_{1}}{k_{-1}}=\dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]^{2}}{[\mathrm{A}{}_{2}]}\Rightarrow [\mathrm{A}]=\left (\dfrac{k_{1}}{k_{-1}}\right )^{1/2}[\mathrm{A}{}_{2}]^{1/2}$

Substituting in the rate law:

$\text{rate}=k_{2}\left (\dfrac{k_{1}}{k_{-1}}\right )^{1/2}[\mathrm{A}{}_{2}]^{1/2}[\mathrm{B}{}_{2}]$

Overall order $=\dfrac{1}{2}+1=1.5$.

Hence, the correct option is (C).

text: If $a_{0}$ is denoted as the Bohr radius of hydrogen atom, then what is the de-Broglie wavelength (λ) of the electron present in the second orbit of hydrogen atom? [n : any integer]
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Bohr radius of hydrogen atom $\to a_{0}$

According to Bohr, the equation used to calculate the angular momentum of an electron in a hydrogen atom is

$\mathrm{mvr}=\frac{\mathrm{nh}}{2π}$ ..... (1)

$m\to$ mass of electron

$v\to$ velocity of electron

$r\to$ radius of the orbit

$n\to$ orbit number in which electron is present.

Given that; electron is present in second orbit, $n=2$

The radius of the second orbit $r_{2}=a_{0}\times 2^{2}=4a_{0}$

General formula for radius of $n^{th}$ orbit,

$r_{n}=a_{0}\times n^{2}$

From (1)

$\begin{array}{l} mvr=n\dfrac{h}{2π} \\ 2πr=n\dfrac{h}{mv} \end{array}$

$\frac{h}{mv}=λ$ (de Broglie relationship, $λ\to$ de Broglie Wavelength

So, $2πr=nλ$

For the electron in the second orbit, $2πr_{2}=nλ$

Substitute for $r_{2}$,

$\begin{array}{l} 2π\times 4a_{0}=nλ \\ 8πa_{0}=nλ \\ \therefore λ=\dfrac{8πa_{0}}{n} \end{array}$

Correct answer: Option 1) $\frac{8πa_{0}}{n}$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift

text:
Choose the correct statements.
(A) Weight of a substance is the amount of matter present in it.
(B) Mass is the force exerted by gravity on an object.
(C) Volume is the amount of space occupied by a substance.
(D) Temperatures below 0°C are possible in Celsius scale, but in Kelvin scale negative temperature is not possible.
(E) Precision refers to the closeness of various measurements for the same quantity.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
A) Weight of a substance is the amount of matter present in it.

Not correct.

The amount of matter present in a substance is called its mass, not its weight.

Mass of a substance is the amount of matter present in it.

B) Mass is the force exerted by gravity on an object.

Not correct.

Mass is not the force exerted on an object by gravity. Mass is the amount of matter in an object, while weight is the force of gravity on that object.

C) Volume is the amount of space occupied by a substance.

Correct.

The amount of space occupied by a substance is its volume, which is simply the equivalent three dimensional measurements of spatial geometry (height, width and length).

Standard units of volume are cubic centimeters for solids, milliliters or liters for liquids, and liters for gases.

D) Temperatures below $0^{\circ }\mathrm{C}$ are possible in Celsius scale, but in Kelvin scale negative temperature is not possible.

Correct.

Celsius temp is possible below $0^{\circ }\mathrm{C}$ (negative temp). But, it is not possible in the Kelvin Scale

$273\mathrm{K}\to$ Absolute temperature

Kelvin temp $={}^{\circ }\mathrm{C}$ temp +273.15

The minimum temperature possible in the Kelvin scale is the absolute zero temperature ($0\mathrm{K}$). 0 K means $-273.15^{\circ }\mathrm{C}$. Since absolute zero is the coldest possible temperature, there are no negative values on the Kelvin temperature scale.

E) Precision refers to the closeness of various measurements for the same quantity.

Correct.

A measure of how close repeated measurements are to each other is known as precision.
Precision is the reproducibility of a result or measurement.

If weight of a substance is measured five times and get 8.2 kg each time, then the measurement is very precise - Example.

So, the correct statements are (C) , (D) and (E).

Correct answer: Option 3) (C) ,(D) and(E) only

text: At temperature T, compound $AB_{2(g)}$ dissociates as $AB_{2(g)}⇌AB_{(g)}+\frac{1}{2}B_{2(g)}$ having degree of dissociation $x$ (small compared to unity). The correct expression for $x$ in terms of $K_{p}$ and $p$ is:
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
$AB_{2}(g)⇌AB_{(g)}+\frac{1}{2}B_{2}(g)$

Degree of dissociation $\to x$ (small compared to unity)

Equilibrium constant in terms of pressure $\to k_{p}$

Partial pressure of each gas $\to P_{AB_{2}},P_{AB}$ and $P_{B_{2}}$

Total pressure $\to P$

ICE Table:


[IMG]


$\begin{array}{l} \text{partial pressure} \\ \text{at equilibrium} \end{array}=\frac{\text{moles at equilibrium}}{\begin{array}{l} \text{total moles at} \\ \text{equilibrium} \end{array}}\times$ total pressure

Partial pressure of $AB_{2}(g)$

$P_{AB_{2}}=\left (\frac{1-x}{1+\frac{x}{2}}\right )P$

Partial pressure of $AB(g)$

$P_{AB}=\left (\frac{x}{1+\frac{x}{2}}\right )P$

Partial pressure of $B_{2}(g)$

$P_{B_{2}}=\left (\frac{\frac{x}{2}}{1+\frac{x}{2}}\right )P$

$K_{p}$ for the equation $AB_{2}(g)⇌AB_{(g)}+\frac{1}{2}B_{2}(g)$ can be written as

$k_{p}=\frac{P_{AB}P_{B2}^{1/2}}{P_{AB2}}$

$\begin{array}{l} =\dfrac{\frac{x}{1+\frac{x}{2}}P1\times \left (\frac{\frac{x}{2}}{1+\frac{x}{2}}P\right )^{1/2}}{\frac{1-x}{1+\frac{x}{2}}P} \\ =\dfrac{x\times \left (\frac{\frac{x}{2}}{1+\frac{x}{2}}P\right )^{1/2}}{1-x} \end{array}$

$\begin{array}{l} \text{given,}x⋘1 \\ \begin{array}{l} \text{So,}1-x\approx 1 \\ K_{p}=\dfrac{x\times \left (\frac{\frac{x}{2}}{1+\frac{x}{2}}p\right )^{1/2}}{1} \end{array} \end{array}$

$=x\times \frac{\left (\frac{x}{2}\right )^{1/2}}{\left (\frac{2+x}{2}\right )^{1/2}}p^{1/2}$

$=\frac{x\times \frac{x1/2}{2 1/2}\times p^{1/2}}{\frac{(2+x)1/2}{2 1/2}}$

$=\frac{x^{3/2}\times p^{1/2}}{2^{1/2}}\times \frac{2^{1/2}}{(2+x)^{1/2}}$

$\begin{array}{l} x⋘1 \\ 2+x\approx 2 \end{array}$

$\begin{array}{l} =\dfrac{x^{3/2}\times p^{1/2}}{2^{1/2}} \\ =\left (\dfrac{x^{3}p}{2}\right )^{1/2} \end{array}$

$\begin{array}{l} k_{p}=\left (\dfrac{x^{3}p}{2}\right )^{1/2} \\ \text{Square on both sides,} \end{array}$

$\begin{array}{ll} k_{p}^{2} & =\dfrac{x^{3}p}{2} \\ x^{3}p & =2k_{p}^{2} \\ x^{3} & =\dfrac{2k_{p}^{2}}{p} \\ x & =\sqrt{3\dfrac{2k_{p}^{2}}{p}} \end{array}$

Correct answer option (2) $\sqrt{3\frac{2K_{p}^{2}}{p}}$

text:
Match List - I with List - II.

  
    List - I (Complex)
    List - II (Hybridisation & Magnetic characters)
  
  
    (A) [MnBr$_{4}$]$^{2-}$
    $(I) d^{2}sp^{3}$ & diamagnetic
  
  
    (B) [FeF$_{6}$]$^{3-}$
    $(II) sp^{3}d^{2}$ & paramagnetic
  
  
    (C) [$Co(C_{2}O_{4})_{3}$]$^{3-}$
    (III$) sp^{3}$ & diamagnetic
  
  
    (D) [$Ni(CO)_{4}$]
    $(IV) sp^{3}$ & paramagnetic
  

Choose the correct answer from the options given below :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
In $[\mathrm{MnBr}{}_{4}]{}^{2-}$ the metal is $\mathrm{Mn}{}^{2+}$ ($3d^{5}$). $\mathrm{Br}{}^{-}$ is a weak-field ligand, so the five 3d electrons stay unpaired and the 4s and 4p orbitals hybridise: tetrahedral $sp^{3}$, paramagnetic ($n=5$), which is (IV).


[IMG]

In $[\mathrm{FeF}{}_{6}]{}^{3-}$ the metal is $\mathrm{Fe}{}^{3+}$ ($3d^{5}$). $\mathrm{F}{}^{-}$ is weak-field, so no pairing occurs and the outer 4s, 4p and 4d orbitals are used: $sp^{3}d^{2}$, paramagnetic ($n=5$), which is (II).


[IMG]

In $[\mathrm{Co}(\mathrm{C}{}_{2}\mathrm{O}{}_{4}){}_{3}]{}^{3-}$ the metal is $\mathrm{Co}{}^{3+}$ ($3d^{6}$). The high charge of $\mathrm{Co}{}^{3+}$ gives a large $\Delta _{o}$ even with oxalate, so $\Delta _{o}>P$ and the six electrons pair up in three 3d orbitals ($t_{2g}^{6}e_{g}^{0}$). Two empty 3d orbitals take part: $d^{2}sp^{3}$, diamagnetic, which is (I).


[IMG]

In $[\mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{CO}){}_{4}]$ nickel is $\mathrm{Ni}{}^{0}$ ($3d^{8}4s^{2}$). Strong-field CO pushes the 4s electrons into 3d, giving $3d^{10}$, and the empty 4s and 4p orbitals hybridise: tetrahedral $sp^{3}$, diamagnetic, which is (III).


[IMG]

So the matching is (A)-(IV), (B)-(II), (C)-(I), (D)-(III).

Hence, the correct option is (C).

solution.body:
Steam volatile compounds can be distilled using steam distillation. Steam volatility is influenced by the intermolecular forces present in the substance. Steam volatile compounds have lower boiling points and weaker intermolecular forces.

A compound's steam volatility is directly related to hydrogen bonding.

The presence of intramolecular hydrogen bonds make a molecule more volatile. A compound's intermolecular hydrogen bonding decreases its volatility.

So, molecules with intramolecular hydrogen bonds are more likely to be steam volatile:

(A) 
[IMG]


Intramolecular hydrogen bonding is present in this molecule.


[IMG]


So, it is steam volatile

(B) 
[IMG]


The $-\mathrm{NH}_{2}$ group and $-\mathrm{NO}_{2}$ group are at ortho positions (adjacent positions) and hence there is intramolecular hydrogen bonding.

The electronegative oxygen of $-\mathrm{NO}_{2}$ group and hydrogen of $-\mathrm{NH}_{2}$ group makes the intramolecular hydrogen bonding. Due to this, intramolecular hydrogen bonding, O-nitroaniline is considered as steam volatile.

(C) 
[IMG]


The amino group and hydroxy group are at para positions and the possibility of intramolecular hydrogen bonding is less in this compound. Therefore, this compound is not considered as steam volatile.

(D) 
[IMG]


The $-\mathrm{NH}_{2}$ group and group are far away to form intramolecular hydrogen bonding. As a result, it is not considered as steam volatile.

The steam volatile compounds are


[IMG]


Correct answer option (3) (A) and (B) only.

Total number of nucleophiles from the following is :

[IMG]
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Nucleophiles are electron rich species and can provide electrons for making new bonds.

Nucleophiles are nucleus loving species

* typically have a $-$ve (negative) charge or non-bonding electron pair available for making a new bond.

Nucleophiles are Lewis bases.

$\mathrm{NH}_{3}$ - It is a nucleophile.

$\mathrm{NH}_{3}$ has a lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom which allows it to be a nucleophile since it can provide electrons to form a new bond.

PhSH - It is a nucleophile

Lone pair of electrons are present on the sulphur atom and hence it is a nucleophile. The lone pair of electrons are readily donated to form new bonds with electrophiles.

$(\mathrm{CH}_{3})_{2}\mathrm{S}$ - It is a nucleophile

The lone pair of electrons on the sulphur atom makes this molecule nucleophile.

$\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{CH}_{2}-$ It is a nucleophile

Alkenes are nucleophiles because they have a high electron density in their carbon-carbon double bond. The $π$ bond in $\mathrm{CH}_{2}=\mathrm{CH}_{2}$ is a region of high electron density.

$O^{\Theta }H$ - It is a nucleophile

Hydroxide ion is a nucleophile, not an electrophile. It is negatively charged and electron rich. The electrons are easily donated.

$\mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{O}^{⊕}$ - It is not a nucleophile

Hydronium ion is an electrophile. It can gain a pair of electrons from a nucleophile. Also, it is positively charged.

$(\mathrm{CH}_{3})_{2}\mathrm{CO}$ - It is not a nucleophile.

Acetone 
[IMG]
 primarily acts as an electrophile in reactions. It can readily accept electron pairs from other molecules due to the partial positive charge on the carbonyl carbon atom.


[IMG]
 - It is not a nucleophile.

It is an imine compound 
[IMG]
 and generally act as electrophile in reactions. The carbon in the $C=N$ double bond is electrophile and attacked by nucleophiles.

So, the nucleophiles are

$\mathrm{NH}_{3},\mathrm{PhSH},(\mathrm{CH}_{3})_{2}\mathrm{S},\mathrm{CH}_{2}=\mathrm{CH}_{2},\mathrm{OH}^{-}$

Total number of nucleophiles is 5

text: An element ‘E’ has the ionisation enthalpy value of 374 kJ mol⁻¹. ‘E’ reacts with elements A, B, C and D with electron gain enthalpy values of −328, −349, −325 and −295 kJ mol⁻¹, respectively. The correct order of the products EA, EB, EC and ED in terms of ionic character is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Element E has a very low ionisation enthalpy ($374\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$, typical of an alkali metal), so it gives up its electron to each of A, B, C and D; the ionic character of EX then depends on how readily X accepts that electron.

The energy needed for $\mathrm{E}(\mathrm{g})\qquad +\mathrm{X}(\mathrm{g})\longrightarrow \mathrm{E}{}^{+}(\mathrm{g})+\mathrm{X}{}^{-}(\mathrm{g})$ is $\Delta _{i}H(\text{E})+\Delta _{eg}H(\text{X})$:

$\text{EB}:374-349=25,\text{EA}:374-328=46,\text{EC}:374-325=49,\text{ED}:374-295=79(\text{kJ mol}^{-1})$

The more negative the electron gain enthalpy of X, the smaller this energy, the more complete the electron transfer and the greater the ionic character:

$\text{EB}>\text{EA}>\text{EC}>\text{ED}$

Hence, the correct option is (A).
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift

text:
Given below are two statements :
Statement (I) : The radii of isoelectronic species increases in the order.

$Mg^{2+}$ Statement (II) : The magnitude of electron gain enthalpy of halogen decreases in the order.

Cl > F > Br > I
In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :
options: Statement I is incorrect but Statement II is correct
Both Statement I and Statement II are correct
Statement I is correct but Statement II is incorrect
Both Statement I and Statement II are incorrect
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
$\mathrm{Mg}{}^{2+}$, $\mathrm{Na}{}^{+}$, $\mathrm{F}{}^{-}$ and $\mathrm{O}{}^{2-}$ each have 10 electrons, with nuclear charges +12, +11, +9 and +8 respectively.

For the same number of electrons, a smaller nuclear charge holds the electron cloud less tightly, so the radius increases as the nuclear charge decreases: $\mathrm{Mg}{}^{2+}<\mathrm{Na}{}^{+}<\mathrm{F}{}^{-}<\mathrm{O}{}^{2-}$. Statement I is correct.

Electron gain enthalpy becomes less negative down group 17, except that F is less negative than Cl, because the incoming electron enters the small, compact 2p subshell of F and suffers strong repulsion. The values are Cl $-349$, F $-328$, Br $-325$ and I $-295\text{kJ mol}^{-1}$, so the magnitude decreases in the order $\mathrm{Cl}>\mathrm{F}>\mathrm{Br}>\mathrm{I}$. Statement II is correct.

Hence, the correct option is (B).
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift

text:
Given below are some nitrogen containing compounds :

[IMG]

Each of them is treated with HCl separately. 1.0 g of the most basic compound will consume $_______ mg$ of HCl.
(Given molar mass in g mol$^{−1} C$ : 12, H : 1, O : 16, Cl : 35.5)
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The four compounds are p-nitroaniline, benzylamine, acetanilide and aniline.

In aniline the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring; in p-nitroaniline the $-\mathrm{NO}{}_{2}$ group withdraws it further; in acetanilide it is delocalised into the $\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{O}$ group of the amide. All three are weak bases.

In benzylamine, $\mathrm{C}{}_{6}\mathrm{H}{}_{5}\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}\mathrm{NH}{}_{2}$, the $-\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}-$ group separates nitrogen from the ring, so the lone pair stays localised and benzylamine is the most basic. It reacts with HCl in a 1 : 1 ratio:

$\mathrm{C}{}_{6}\mathrm{H}{}_{5}\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}\mathrm{NH}{}_{2}+\mathrm{HCl}\longrightarrow \mathrm{C}{}_{6}\mathrm{H}{}_{5}\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}\mathrm{NH}{}_{3}{}^{+}\mathrm{Cl}{}^{-}$


[IMG]

Molar mass of $\mathrm{C}{}_{7}\mathrm{H}{}_{9}\mathrm{N}=7(12)+9(1)+14=107\text{g mol}^{-1}$, so $n=\dfrac{1.0}{107}=9.35\times 10^{-3}\text{mol}$.

Mass of HCl $=9.35\times 10^{-3}\times 36.5=0.341\text{g}=341\text{mg}$.

Hence, the answer is 341.

text: If $A_{2}B$ is 30% ionised in an aqueous solution, then the value of van't Hoff factor (i) is $_______ × 10^{−1}$.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Percent ionisation of $A_{2}B=30%$

The dissociation of $A_{2}B$ in aqueous solution can be represented as

$A_{2}B\to 2A^{+}+B^{2-}$

1 mole of $A_{2}B$ produces 2 moles of $A^{+}$ and 1 mole of $B^{2-}$ ions.

The total number of moles of ions produced (n) from the dissociation is

$n=2+1=3$

The degree of dissociation given that $A_{2}B$ is 30% ionised, the degree of dissociation $(λ)$ or degree of ionisation

$λ=\frac{30}{100}=0.3$

Van't Hoff factor ($i$) can be calculated using the formula,

$i=1+(n-1)λ$

Substitute the values of $n$ and $λ$ as,

$i=1+(3-1)\times 0.3$

$=1+2\times 0.3$

$=1+0.6$

$=1.6$

$=16\times 10^{-1}$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2025 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift

text:
[IMG]

0.1 mole of compound ‘S’ will weigh $___________ g$.
(Given molar mass in g mol$^{−1} C$ : 12, H : 1, O : 16)
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2025 (Online) 29th January Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The substrate is 2-(hydroxymethyl)cyclopentan-1-ol. Excess $\mathrm{CrO}{}_{3}$ (anhydrous) oxidises the secondary OH to a ketone and the primary $\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}\mathrm{OH}$ to $\mathrm{CHO}$, so P is 2-oxocyclopentane-1-carbaldehyde.

One mole of ethane-1,2-diol with $\mathrm{H}{}^{+}$ reacts with the more reactive aldehyde group and converts it into a cyclic acetal (1,3-dioxolane), leaving the ketone free in Q.

$\mathrm{CH}{}_{3}\mathrm{MgI}$ adds to the ketone; $\mathrm{H}{}_{3}\mathrm{O}{}^{+}$ then protonates the alkoxide to a tertiary alcohol and hydrolyses the acetal back to $\mathrm{CHO}$, so R is 2-hydroxy-2-methylcyclopentane-1-carbaldehyde.

$\mathrm{NaBH}{}_{4}$ reduces $\mathrm{CHO}$ to $\mathrm{CH}{}_{2}\mathrm{OH}$, so S is 2-(hydroxymethyl)-1-methylcyclopentan-1-ol, $\mathrm{C}{}_{7}\mathrm{H}{}_{14}\mathrm{O}{}_{2}$.

Molar mass of S $=7(12)+14(1)+2(16)=130\text{g mol}^{-1}$, so $0.1$ mol weighs $0.1\times 130=13\text{g}$.

Hence, the answer is 13.

solution.body:
The compound given is hex-1,3-dien-5-yne structure is


[IMG]


A doble bond has one $π$ bond and one sigma bond.

A triple bond has one sigma bond and two $π$ bonds.

For the one triple bond, number of $π$ bonds = 2

For one double bond, number of $π$ bond = 1

For two double bonds, number of $π$ bonds = 2

So, total number of $π$ bonds = 2 + 2 = 4

For sigma bonds, count all carbon - carbon bonds and carbon - hydrogen bonds except the $π$ bonds in double bonds and triple bond.


[IMG]


The total number of sigma bonds = 11

So, total number of bonds:

$σ=11$

$π=4$

Sum of $σ$ and $π$ bonds

$=11+4=15$
